Isobar Industries

Polymorphic comb and mutation engine. Nine ways to make a delay line ring, nine ways to mutate a signal, on a single feedback loop.

Working draft. Still to come: the final patches, the comb and mutation ring graphics, the default-position illustrations, and the depth and current-draw figures.

Introduction.

Serratus is a stereo comb filter and mutation engine. One of nine comb algorithms excites the input through a pitched feedback loop. One of nine mutations, a stereo filter and a reverb, can sit before that loop, inside it, or after it. Both banks can step or morph from one algorithm into the next.

Conventions.

Knob positions use clock notation. 7:00 is fully counter-clockwise, 12:00 is centered, 5:00 is fully clockwise. A bipolar knob rests at noon. Control names are written in capitals, or as the symbol on the panel where one is used. Buttons appear in brackets, like [Freeze]. Jacks are named by their panel labels. Combs and mutations are numbered with roman numerals, I to IX, the same as the panel.

Front panel.

Knobs

Pitch
The comb's note, across ten octaves. An endless knob. Its LED ring shows two comets: one marks the octave you are in, the other the pitch within that octave, completing a full lap of the ring for each octave. In Clock mode the knob selects a clock ratio instead.
Feed*
Feedback amount and polarity. Right of noon is positive, left is inverted, noon is silent. Around 3 o'clock the loop self-oscillates.
Orbit
Orbital feedback. A second endless knob, a full 360 degree rotation, that sets a stereo crossfeed angle inside the loop.
Matter*
Material damping of the feedback, from Rubber (dark) through Neutral to Crystal-bright. Bipolar.
Ebb*
The comb's spectral character, what it rings with. Its meaning changes per algorithm.
Flow*
The comb's temporal character, how it rings. Its meaning changes per algorithm.
Rend*
A mutation character knob, broadly the intensity. Each mutation reads it its own way.
Bind*
A mutation character knob, broadly the character. Each mutation reads it its own way.
Etch*
The filter, bipolar in both modes. A DJ filter or a 16-band filterbank, chosen by a toggle switch on the panel.
Q*
Etch resonance in the DJ filter, band Q in the filterbank.
Melt*
Reverb, bipolar. Ore (dark plate reverb) to the left, Aer (bright +-1 octave shimmer reverb) to the right, off at noon.
Seep*
Reverb decay and size, moved together.
Leech*
The self-modulation system, bipolar. Organismic (reactive) right, chaotic (restless) left, off at noon.
In Lvl
Input gain, trimming around an automatic baseline. Unity at noon.
Mix
Dry to wet.

* marks a control you can assign to the internal envelope mod bus. See Mod bus.

Toggle Switches

  • V/Oct, Clock. How the Pitch jack is read: a V/Oct pitch voltage across ten octaves, or a clock that the Pitch knob then divides and multiplies.
  • Mutation route. Mutation before the comb, inside it, or after it.
  • Reverb route. The reverb before the comb, inside the loop, or after it.
  • Etch route. Etch before the comb, inside the loop, or after it.
  • Etch mode. DJ filter or filterbank.

Buttons

  • [Freeze] captures and loops the buffer.
  • [Lock] sets the pitch mode when presand locks pitch.
  • [Mod] runs the envelope follower and its modulation bus.
  • The two encoder pushes mute and morph their banks (see The matrix and Gestures).

Default positions

Signal path.

Serratus is one feedback loop with three movable inserts. Knowing where the mutation, reverb, and Etch sit on that loop is the difference between a sound that bites and one that shimmers.

The input passes through the input gain stage and splits. One branch stays dry and goes to Mix. The other enters the comb loop, where Pitch sets the delay length, Feed sets the loop gain, and Matter filters what survives each pass. The three inserts can each sit at one of three points:

  • PRE. Before the comb, on the input branch.
  • MID. Inside the feedback loop, applied on every pass. The wildest territory, and the one that rewards a careful Feed setting.
  • POST. After the comb's wet output, on its way to Mix.

The switches are independent, so a mutation can run pre while the reverb runs post and Etch runs inside the loop. Changing a route triggers a short volume dip that hides the switch.

You do not have to lean on both halves at once. Put the mutation PRE and turn Feed down, and the combs pass an almost dry signal you are mostly mutating; turn the mutation off and the comb is the whole voice. They are built to interlock, but either can sit in the background.

The matrix.

Two encoders, two banks of nine. The comb encoder runs one axis, nine ways to make a delay line ring. The mutation encoder runs the other, nine ways to mutate a sample. Eighty-one named intersections, and the whole continuum between them. Every comb pairs with every mutation.

Each encoder works two ways. In step mode, one detent lands one algorithm. Hold the encoder to switch it into morph mode: now three detents span each algorithm and the encoder crossfades continuously between neighbors, parkable mid-blend and drivable from the matching CV input. A short click mutes the cursor's current algorithm. It keeps sounding while the cursor sits on it, but is skipped the next time you navigate past it, so muting several lets the encoder step only through the ones you keep. You can mute all but one, and you can always land the cursor back on a muted algorithm to bring it back.

Where a mutation sits relative to the comb, before it, inside the loop, or after it, is set by its route switch: it can shape the input, the resonance on every pass, or the output. See Signal path.

Combs.

Nine ways to build a resonant delay. In every algorithm, Pitch sets the loop's period, the note, across ten octaves, and Feed sets how long it rings. Feed is bipolar: right of noon is positive feedback, left inverts the loop for a more hollow, odd-harmonic voice, and around 3 o'clock the loop self-oscillates and rings without any input. What changes from algorithm to algorithm is the pair Ebb and Flow. Ebb is what the comb rings with; Flow is how it rings.

IFractured Prism

Stretched strings, and glass pulling apart.

A delay tap pushed through a four-stage allpass cascade that bends each frequency's travel time. High partials arrive a few samples late, so the harmonic series smears into bell-like, glassy inharmonicity that builds with every pass.

Feed
Decay. Left of noon inverts the loop for a thinner, glassier ring.
Ebb
Dispersion depth. Low is a clean delay, harmonically pure; high is full group-delay smear and glassy inharmonicity.
Flow
Per-stage spread. Noon is a uniform, chorus-like smear; toward either extreme the stages diverge into a bell-shaped dispersion curve.

IIFilamentum

A struck or bowed string, modeled.

A bidirectional waveguide: two traveling-wave delay lines reflecting at a bridge and a nut, with a movable pickup. It wants a transient to excite it. Pluck it with a click, bow it with anything sustained.

Feed
Round-trip gain: how much energy comes back on each pass.
Ebb
How much the string's end soaks up. Against intuition, high Ebb damps more, for a shorter, less ringing tone; low Ebb lets the reflections run.
Flow
How tightly the string is anchored, and where the pickup sits along it. Low is loose and fluttery; high is tight and defined.

IIIPerpetuum

A loop that refuses to die quietly.

A comb with an automatic gain control inside the loop. As the ring fades, the control pushes it back toward a threshold, and a trace of noise keeps it alive even in silence. Loop gain can pass unity without running away. Can give its feedback a sidechaining effect.

Feed
Drive into the loop. Past 3 o'clock it self-sustains as a breathing, pumping drone in its own right.
Ebb
Control speed. Low breathes slowly; high grabs transients fast and chirps.
Flow
Knee and asymmetry. Low is a hard knee and symmetric saturation; high adds a soft knee and a warm offset that loads in even harmonics.

IVEmpyrean Cascade

Bells, bars, struck metal.

Four tuned modal resonators in series, driven in parallel by the delay tap. Highly pitch-stable. You hear the clean delay tap, with the modal bank coloring only the feedback.

Feed
Ring time. Long Feed sustains the bell; short Feed thuds.
Ebb
Tuning. A pure harmonic series at the bottom, sliding to stiff, inharmonic bell ratios at the top.
Flow
Liveness. Decay spread between the modes plus coupling, so partials take turns being dominant.

VOiler

A seasick electro-mechanical echo.

A model of the Tel-Ray oil-can delay. A clean tap plus a wobbled tap whose delay, level, and tone all ride one rotating disc. The rotation tracks the note now, so the warble follows pitch instead of sitting at one rate, and it speeds up when you play harder.

Feed
Regeneration, how many times the disc re-reads itself.
Ebb
Rotation rate, plus a broken-bearing second harmonic in the wobble and how strongly the input's rhythm drives the disc.
Flow
Warble depth and the balance of wobbled against clean tap. A faint breath at the bottom, full character at the top.

VIPneuma

Half breath, half voice, from a whisper to a scream.

A breathing, voice-like resonator built as a comb. Inside the loop sits a sprung reed that beats against pressure, with a vocal tract folded into the feedback. Feed it any sound and it rings at the Pitch note with a living, formant-rich color, and the input's own dynamics blow it: play harder and it breathes harder.

Feed
Decay, and it self-oscillates around 3 o'clock with an attack and decay rather than a static sine wave. The polarity of Feed matters more than usual here: to the right the voice is full, with every harmonic; to the left it hollows out, odd harmonics only, an octave lower.
Ebb
Extended-technique morph. Subtone whisper counter-clockwise, through a straight voice, into a growl, then multiphonic split-tones clockwise.
Flow
Breath and air: reed pressure and the amount of wind in the tone.

VIIStochastic Automaton

A delay played by something that is not you.

Eight taps spread across five octaves, gated by a one-dimensional cellular automaton that steps in time with the pitch. A noise-assisted threshold sets how strongly each active tap rings. Alive, and never quite the same twice.

Feed
Decay of each struck tap.
Ebb
Rule and speed. Sweeps eight cellular-automaton rules from periodic through complex to chaotic, evolving faster as you turn up.
Flow
Noise level and tap release. Low is flickery, percussive switching; high blooms and sustains as the noise lifts the weak taps over their threshold.

VIIICataract

A transient unfolding into a wobbly frequency-staggered cloud.

A long cascade of allpass filters in series with the delay, giving strong frequency-dependent group delay. A single attack unfurls into a spectral waterfall.

Feed
Decay. High Feed turns the dispersed cloud into a sustained, drifting wash.
Ebb
Chirp. The sign sets direction, left descending and right ascending; the distance from center sets intensity.
Flow
Clean to dispersed mix. Low keeps attacks sharp; high smears them into spectral waterfalls.

IXGravity Warp

Bell to fog in one sweep.

Four taps that compress or stretch around the fundamental, plus a sub-octave tap for body, all run through a diffusion chain. The sub-octave bleed is what gives this one its weight.

Feed
Decay across the tap cluster.
Ebb
Tap spread and sub-octave mix. Low clusters the taps near unison; high spreads them into inharmonic bell ratios and deepens the sub.
Flow
Diffusion. Low keeps tap transients defined; high washes the tap sum into a reverberant smear.

Mutations.

Nine ways to mutate a sample. Some are distortions, some are stranger. The mutation encoder selects the algorithm, and two knobs shape it: Rend is broadly the intensity, Bind broadly the character, though each algorithm reads them in its own way. There is no separate drive knob; the character knobs carry it. Where a mutation sits relative to the comb is set by its route switch. Inside the loop, on MID, it is re-applied on every pass and becomes part of the resonance.

ITransformer Sat

Iron, warmth, weight in the low mids.

A saturator that splits low from high and pushes the low harder, the way an iron transformer core does, while the top is softened separately. Useful in front to thicken a source, or after to glue the output.

Rend
Drive. More Rend pins the low path further into saturation and gently rolls the very top.
Bind
Asymmetry. Off-centers the waveform before saturation to load in even harmonics.

IIStarved Tube

A tube fed too little voltage.

A waveshaper whose bias sags under load, the way a starved plate supply droops. Quiet signals stay clean; loud sustained ones pull back and break up.

Rend
Sag. How far the bias drifts under a loud signal, which reads as compression and sustain.
Bind
Drive and bias. Static gain and a fixed offset, asymmetric, for even-harmonic grit.

IIIHeterodyne

Tremolo at the bottom, ring-mod at the top.

An amplitude-modulation (AM) distortion: the signal multiplied by an internal oscillator. Slow, it is tremolo. Fast, it is full AM, throwing off sum and difference sidebands with no fixed musical relationship to the input.

Rend
Oscillator frequency, from a fraction of a hertz up to a few kilohertz.
Bind
Oscillator shape, sine through triangle to square.

IVPlasma Arc

Crackle and sputter, not fuzz.

A model of an electric arc. Once the signal ignites the gap, the voltage drops to a sustain level and decays with hysteresis, with ignition jitter and a louder avalanche on peaks. It crackles and re-strikes rather than clipping.

Rend
Ignition threshold and depth. Low is occasional and gentle; high is a continuous plasma roar.
Bind
Ionization memory, from a brief one-shot to a long, chaotic re-firing.

VStrata Fold

West-coast wavefolding.

A wavefolder with a morphing rectifier in front. The wave folds back on itself instead of clipping, so harmonics multiply with drive while the level stays roughly constant. The fundamental survives, so it stays musical.

Rend
Rectification and fold gain. Sweeps the rectifier and drives the folds harder.
Bind
Fold threshold. Wide folds less; narrow folds more, for dense upper harmonics.

VIOctave Fuzz

An octave up, screaming.

An octave-up rectifier feeding a hard gain stage and soft clip. The octave layer tracks the input, so it sings with melodic material.

Rend
Drive, from clean through heavy gain.
Bind
Octave blend. Subtle low, dominant high, mixing the rectified octave into the drive.

VIIJPEG Codec

Image compression artifacts as a waveshaper.

A wavefolder run through the math of a heavily compressed JPEG. The signal is folded, then quantized the way a codec posterizes an image, with the ringing halo you get around the hard edges in a bad JPEG and a square-wave octave underneath. It is mostly wavefolder, with a little sample reduction on top, not a bitcrusher: blocky and ringing in a way nothing else here is.

Rend
Ringing band. Sweeps the center of the edge-halo filter from low to high, moving where the artifacts sing.
Bind
Compression depth. Coarsens the palette from many levels down to a few, raising the drive and the fold as it goes; high Bind is a heavily crushed, muffled image.

VIIIWaveset

Single cycles, rearranged.

Works on wavesets, the single cycles between zero crossings, rather than on samples. It records them and plays them back stretched, reversed, or thinned out, so the pitch is preserved while the timbre is bent out of shape.

Rend
Playback rate and direction, from half speed (an octave down) through normal to double speed and reversed.
Bind
Density. How many wavesets are affected, from every one to roughly one in eight.

IXGlossa

A throat growing around the signal.

The input drives a voice: a pulse generator and closure noise, gated by the input envelope and shaped through a model of a vocal tract. Speech-like material is hollowed and vocoded; other material grows a throat. It makes no sound when the input is silent.

Rend
Voice intensity, from a light shaped passthrough to full pulse and noise.
Bind
Chaos. Sub-harmonics and pulse jitter that push the voice toward biphonation.

Reverb.

One reverb with two voices, chosen on Melt. Melt rests at noon, where the reverb is off. Turn it counter-clockwise for Ore, clockwise for Aer; the further from noon, the wetter.

Melt
The reverb control, bipolar. It picks the voice and sets the wet level at once: noon is dry with the reverb off, counter-clockwise fades up Ore, and clockwise fades up Aer. The further from noon, the wetter the tail.
Ore
A dark, full, plate-like room. The main reverb.
Aer
A shimmer. Pitch shifters inside the tank run an octave up and an octave down at once, so every regeneration adds an ascending sparkle and a descending bloom.
Seep
Decay and size for either voice. It leans on the comb's feedback, so the tail breathes with the ring.

Matter biases the brightness of the tail. Crossing Melt through noon swaps voices cleanly, with no leftover from the previous one. Reverb has its own route switch; placed before the comb it feeds a wash into the resonance, placed inside the loop it accumulates on every pass.

Etch.

Etch is the filter, set by the Etch mode switch: a DJ filter and a filterbank, with a main cut knob and a Q knob.

DJ filter
Left of noon takes off the top, right of noon thins the bottom, noon is flat, down to a firm cut but never silent. Q adds a resonant edge at the corner.
Filterbank
Sixteen bands on the Bark scale, from the low bass to the top of hearing. The lowest and highest bands are shelves, so the extremes pass rather than being rejected. Etch transposes the whole bank by up to half an octave; Q sweeps it from a broad spectral tilt to a tuned set of sixteen resonators. Low and mid bands are split slightly left and right for width.

Etch has its own route switch. Inside the loop at high Q in filterbank mode it becomes an aggressive, self-feeding resonator.

Freeze.

[Freeze] captures a short loop, the length of the current delay, and plays it back in place of the input. Press again to release. A gate at the Freeze jack does the same, following the gate rather than toggling.

While frozen, the rest of the panel still works. Move Pitch and the held sound pitches; sweep the encoders and a different algorithm processes it.

Hold [Freeze] while frozen to latch an edit mode. Ebb, Flow, Rend, and Bind become relative controls over the loop, scrubbing the read position, detuning the two sides, wandering, and setting how long it sustains, while the comb holds its settings. Press and hold [Freeze] again to leave the freeze-edit mode.

Each of the four knobs takes on a freeze function:

KnobFreeze functionWhat it does
EbbScrubPlayback position through the frozen buffer. Noon = middle; sweep it to scan/scrub through the captured audio.
FlowDetuneFine L/R detune of the playback. 0 = clean; dial up for subtle beating / chorus / stereo widening.
RendWanderScrub drift. 0 = the scrub position holds still; dial up and the position drifts/breathes on its own.
BindSustain / thicken0 = static freeze; dial up to thicken and sustain the loop (blends in slightly pitch-shifted/detuned layers).

Leech.

Leech is a single bipolar knob that sets the module modulating itself, a small nervous system wired across the voice. Noon is off, with a deadzone wide enough to ignore knob and voltage jitter. Turn either way and that side's modulation ramps in over a few seconds, so there is no jump as it engages, and it deepens the further you go. The Leech jack is bipolar around zero volts and can reach a side on its own.

Leech touches feedback, damping, Ebb, Flow, the orbital angle, both mutation knobs, the reverb, and Etch. It leaves Pitch, Mix, and input level alone, so the module stays in tune and at level while everything else drifts. The two sides are different types of modulators.

Organismic

Clockwise. A reactive, biological modulation that listens to the input and to your hands. It breathes slowly, leans into playing dynamics, and follows the way you move the knobs, drifting parameters the way a living thing shifts its weight. Musical and unhurried; it makes a patch feel awake rather than random.

Chaotic

Counter-clockwise. Deterministic chaos in layers: a slow drift that unfolds over minutes, a faster chaotic oscillator beneath it, and a slow re-seeding underneath that, so the motion wanders and never repeats. More restless and less predictable than the organismic side, and the place to go when you want a patch that will not sit still.

Mod bus.

The envelope follower has two jobs. It drives the CV output jack, and it can be routed internally to almost any parameter, as if you had patched it to that knob's input with an attenuverter.

Envelope modes

Tap [Mod] to cycle five shapes. The button's LED shows which one is active.

Regular
Smooth tracking of the output. LED amber.
Slewed
A slow, breathing follower. LED orange.
Ping
A sharp attack and a fast decay, like a plucked envelope. LED green.
Gate
A hard on and off at a threshold. LED cyan.
Sidechain
Inverted, so it ducks with the signal. LED magenta.

The chosen shape feeds both the CV output and the internal routing.

Assigning

Hold [Mod] to enter assign mode. While held, every eligible knob becomes an attenuverter for the envelope into that destination: noon is no modulation, clockwise is positive, counter-clockwise is negative. Turn as many knobs as you like in one hold. Knob values freeze during the hold and catch up smoothly on release, so nothing jumps.

The eleven destinations are the controls marked with a star on the panel:

  • Feed, the feedback
  • Matter, material damping
  • Ebb, comb spectral character
  • Flow, comb temporal character
  • Rend, mutation character
  • Bind, mutation character
  • Melt, reverb voice and amount
  • Seep, reverb decay
  • Etch, the filter cut
  • Q, Etch resonance
  • Leech, self-modulation depth

In Lvl and Mix are left out on purpose. To clear every routing, tap [Lock] while holding [Mod]; to clear one, assign its knob back to noon. While you assign, the destination LEDs show the routing depth, and in normal play each parameter's LED follows its modulated value, so you can watch the envelope work.

Pitch and Orbit will become destinations too. That routing is still in development.

Orbital feedback.

Orbit is the second endless knob, a full 360 degree rotation with no stop in either direction. It sets an angle rather than a level, and that angle crossfeeds the left and right channels inside the feedback loop. At the home position there is no crossfeed and the stereo image is normal; its LED marks home in teal. Turn away from home and the channels begin to cross, fullest at the quarter turns, with the half turn reading as a phase inversion. Because it is endless, you can keep rotating through these states as a continuous gesture, and because Leech can drive the angle, the stereo field can rotate on its own.

Aeolian self exciter.

When the input goes quiet for about half a second, Serratus starts to play itself. A synthetic source fades in at the comb's input, a kind of wind across strings, and the comb rings it at the current pitch. Real signal coming back in fades it out again, so the module hands the voice back to you the moment you feed it something. Every knob works on the self-played voice exactly as it would on an input, and Leech adds drift and life.

Gestures.

The complete set of button and encoder gestures.

Freeze + tapFreeze on or off.
Freeze + hold (frozen)Latch freeze-edit mode.
Freeze gateFollows the gate, high freezes.
Lock + tapCycle pitch mode: Free, Semitone, Octave.
Lock + holdPitch lock on or off.
Mod + tapCycle envelope mode.
Mod + holdEnter mod-assign mode.
Mod hold + In Lvl turnWrite the hidden output trim.
Mod hold + Lock tapClear all modulation routings.
Encoder + clickMute or unmute the bank's current algorithm.
Encoder + holdToggle step and morph for that bank.

Pitch modes: Free is continuous. Semitone and Octave snap to an equal-tempered grid anchored at A4 equals 440 Hz, so the same knob position lands on the same note in either quantized mode.

Installation.

Serratus is a 24 HP Eurorack module. Power the case down before fitting it. The power header is not marked −12 V; it carries a RED label instead. Align the ribbon's red stripe with that RED mark, which is the −12 V side. Fit the panel screws and power up. The LEDs run a short start sequence and settle within a second.

Depth and current draw are listed in Specifications once measured on the final build.

Calibration.

Input level is handled by an automatic baseline; In Lvl trims around it, with unity at noon. Pitch tracking over V/Oct is calibrated per unit at the factory. The pitch quantize modes, Free, Semitone, and Octave, are selected with a tap of [Lock] and need no setup.

Specifications.

FormatEurorack, 24 HP
DepthTo confirm on the final build
Power+12 V and −12 V; no +5 V required

Bipolar, ±5 VPitch (V/Oct), Etch, Rend, Bind, Ebb, Flow, Feed, In Lvl, Matter, Leech

Gate inFreeze

ProtectionEvery input is hard-clamped and tolerates out-of-range voltage

In Clock mode the Pitch jack reads a rising-edge clock instead of a pitch voltage.
